apple.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is never the limiter here: the cooler Ozark and upland north banks roughly 1,000 to 1,300 chilling hours a year (University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Chilling Hour Reports; Fayetteville about 1,024), clearing the entire canonical variety range, including the highest-chill selection, McIntosh at about 900 hours, with room to spare. The real risk in a mild winter spell is premature bloom that a later hard freeze can then damage, not a chill shortfall.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Apples do very well here, with an even colder, more reliable winter than the lowland South. The bigger worry than winter cold is an early warm spell tricking the tree into blooming too soon.

Only on the belt's southwestern warm edge, near Hope at about 901 hours, does the margin narrow to about an hour over the highest-chill variety, McIntosh, so favor lower-chill selections there. The real risk is a warm spell pushing bloom too early, ahead of a later freeze, not a lack of winter chill.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Apples grow well here, and winters give nearly every variety the chill it needs; in the region's warmest southwestern corner, lean toward lower-chill varieties to be safe. A warm spell in late winter is a bigger worry than not enough cold.

apricot.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Apricot is marginal here, and the limiting factor is not chill (which clears with room to spare, roughly 1,000 to 1,300 hours a year in zone 7) but fruiting reliability: this tree blooms earlier than any other stone fruit in this guide, often before the region's own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is a frequent event, not an occasional one. Brown rot pressure is also higher in this humid climate than in a drier growing region. Expect the tree to grow well and to fruit in good years, but do not count on a reliable annual crop; site it on a slope or high ground with good cold-air drainage to improve the odds.
7.suitability_note_beginner: This tree is a bit of a gamble here. Winters are cold enough, so chill is not the problem; the issue is its very early bloom, often before your last frost date, which puts a late cold snap right on the flowers most years. It will grow and can fruit in good years, but do not expect a crop every year. Plant it on a slope, not a low spot where cold air pools, to improve your odds.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This tree tends to bloom before the zone 7 (Ozark uplands interior)'s own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is the main frost risk to watch, more than winter cold hardiness.

fig.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is never the limiter here: the belt delivers roughly 1,000 to 1,300 chilling hours a year in zone 7, clearing this crop's variety range with margin (University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Chilling Hour Reports). Chill is not a concern (figs need only about 100 hours), and the real limiter is winter cold hardiness of the aboveground wood in a hard zone 7 winter. A severe freeze can kill the top back to the ground, but the plant typically resprouts from the roots and can still fruit that same season or the next, especially on cold-hardy cultivars like Chicago Hardy, Celeste, and Brown Turkey.

pomegranate.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7's winter lows sit at this crop's cold edge: standard pomegranate wood can be damaged or killed back in a hard freeze, so cold-hardy cultivars (Salavatski, Kazake) on a warm, sheltered, hot-summer site are the reliable path, and even those crop best in a mild winter followed by a hot summer. Chill is never the issue (the crop needs only about 100 hours); winter cold and this belt's own summer humidity both cap the crop below fully reliable.
7.suitability_note_beginner: This is a stretch in the cooler part of the region: a hard winter freeze can kill the top of the plant. Pick a cold-hardy variety and a warm, sheltered spot if you want to try it here.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze most winters, not just an occasional cold snap, is the real threat to the top growth here; a plant frozen back usually resprouts but loses that year's crop.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The lowland South's milder winters ease the cold-hardiness risk that limits zone 7, but this belt's humidity and summer rainfall still cap fruit quality: wet spells split ripening fruit and raise disease pressure, the same limiting pattern Deep South and Gulf Coast growers see. Chill and heat are both ample; humidity, not cold, is the main constraint on this zone's fruit.
8.suitability_note_beginner: This will grow here, but our humid summers and rain can split the fruit and invite disease. It is not a sure thing the way it is in a hot, dry climate.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Winter cold is milder here than in zone 7, but an unusually hard freeze can still damage exposed new growth on this crop.

A cold-hardy cultivar on a warm, sheltered, well-drained site is the reliable path if you want to grow it here.
